name: Social Media and Media Consent
title: Social Media and Media Consent
answer: Social media and media consent means using AI to help draft school posts and design graphics while keeping a strict human check on student photos. Before any student image appears in a post, newsletter, or website, the school must confirm that the family has given permission. This matters because some families opt out for safety reasons, and a mistake can put a child at risk.

sections.body: Schools use social media to share news and celebrations, and AI can help staff draft posts and design graphics in Canva for Education. Scheduling tools can plan posts ahead, which saves time for the people who manage communications. The content should still reflect the school's real life and voice, not a generic feed. The problem this solves is workload, but it also creates a new duty to handle student images carefully. Consent is the central control, because photos of students require permission before they appear in a post, newsletter, or website.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, staff can use AI to draft post text and create graphics, then use scheduling tools to plan when posts go out. Before any student's photo is used in a post, newsletter, or website, the school must confirm that the family has given permission. Some families opt out for safety reasons, including custody disputes or protective orders, so the check has to be reliable. The text does not give separate steps by grade band, so the same consent check applies wherever student photos are used. Schools should also think carefully about how many student photos they post and where they post them.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. It does refer to Chapter 3, which described the TAKE IT DOWN Act, as context for the risk that photos posted online can be taken and altered, including into harmful fakes. That reference is a legal and safety concern, not a research finding. The practical claims here are about saving staff time and protecting students through consent.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are clear: photos of students require consent, and before any student's photo appears in a post, newsletter, or website, the school must confirm that the family has given permission. Some families opt out for safety reasons, including custody disputes or protective orders, and a mistake here can put a child at risk. AI raises new concerns about student images because photos posted online can be taken and altered, including into harmful fakes. The text notes that Chapter 3 described the TAKE IT DOWN Act, which makes sharing intimate deepfakes a crime. Decisions about consent, how many student photos to post, and where to post them stay with people at the school, not with the AI tool.
